Adsorbent / material: Biochar and modified biochar; review-level coverage
Experimental design / conditions: Narrative review; no original adsorption experiment in this paper.
Reported result: The review summarizes biochar modification routes and adsorption of antibiotics and ARGs, with molecular imprinting and biochar aging highlighted; it discusses performance, factors, mechanisms and research challenges.
Model / metric: Review-level synthesis; not a measured result
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 1 (abstract and keywords); PDF p. 2 (contents/section outline)
Caveat / follow-up: Use for field mapping and backward/forward citation chasing only. Do not treat its tables or reported capacities as primary experimental evidence; trace every quantitative claim to the cited original study. Keep antibiotic adsorption separate from ARG adsorption.

Experimental design / conditions: Review outline identifies mechanisms and operating factors covered across cited literature.
Reported result: The review organizes antibiotic adsorption mechanisms under π–π electron-donor–acceptor interactions, electrostatic interactions, surface complexation, pore filling, hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding and ion exchange; operating factors include pH, temperature, initial concentration and coexisting substances.
Model / metric: Review taxonomy, not a validated universal mechanism list
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanism attribution for a specific adsorbent must be supported by its primary study. The review distinguishes ARG adsorption mechanisms from antibiotic adsorption mechanisms.

Adsorbent / material: Haematite, goethite, kaolinite, bentonite, lateritic soil clay, kaolinitic soil clay and illitic soil clay
Continuum stage: Natural minerals / clay interaction; environmental-fate evidence
Experimental design / conditions: Mineral/clay suspensions at 1000 mg/L; OTC at 0, 5, 10 and 20 mg/L; pH varied; ionic strength held at 0.01 M; zeta potential and hydrodynamic diameter measured.
Reported result: Increasing pH and OTC concentration generally shifted zeta potential to more negative values for haematite, goethite, lateritic soil clay, kaolinite and kaolinitic soil clay. Changes for bentonite and illitic soil clay were less apparent. Authors interpret the responses as differing interactions between OTC and mineral surfaces.
Value / units: No single qmax or removal percentage reported for this experiment
Model / metric: Zeta potential (ζ), hydrodynamic diameter (dh); not an isotherm-derived qmax
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2 (Methods); PDF p. 3, Fig. 1 and associated results
Caveat / follow-up: This is sorption/colloid transport and environmental-fate research, not a developed adsorbent-treatment process. Do not convert zeta-potential shifts into a numerical adsorption capacity.

Adsorbent / material: Natural soil clays (lateritic, kaolinitic and illitic) and mineral colloids
Continuum stage: Natural minerals / clay interaction; solution-chemistry evidence
Experimental design / conditions: Mineral/soil-clay suspensions at 1000 mg/L; OTC at 0 or 10 mg/L; deionized water and NaCl conditions of 0.035%, 0.35% and 3.5% representing freshwater, brackish water and seawater; approximately neutral pH; transmittance at 600 nm recorded every 6 min for 6 h; colloid state illustrated after 2 h.
Reported result: Increasing salinity compressed colloidal double layers, promoted aggregation and changed dispersion of soil clays. Authors propose that high salt can compete at mineral surface-exchange sites and intensify release of previously sorbed OTC while remaining OTC can coaggregate with suspended clays.
Model / metric: Time-resolved transmission; visual aggregation state; Fig. 2(c) labelled comparative sorption capacities
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2 (Methods); PDF p. 4, Fig. 2(a–c) and caption
Evidence status: Extracted from supplied primary PDF and figure visually inspected
Caveat / follow-up: The main-text Methods do not clearly explain the direct assay/calculation for the mg/kg values in Fig. 2(c); supplementary Table S1 is referenced but was not supplied. Do not transcribe exact bar values or use a capacity ranking until the calculation/SI is verified.

Adsorbent / material: Illitic, kaolinitic and lateritic soil clays; Fe oxides and silicate minerals
Continuum stage: Natural minerals / clay interaction; environmental fate
Experimental design / conditions: Interpretation of zeta-potential and colloidal-dispersion results under variable pH and salinity.
Reported result: The authors discuss electrostatic attraction to variable-charge mineral/edge sites, possible inner-sphere complexation for Fe-oxide-rich material, and interlayer association/intercalation for bentonite. They propose that salinity can alter colloid aggregation and OTC partitioning/transport.
Value / units: Not quantified as a single mechanism fraction
Model / metric: Mechanistic interpretation based on surface-charge/colloid observations and cited literature
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3–4, Results and discussion; Figs. 1–2
Caveat / follow-up: These are author interpretations, not proof that one mechanism dominates in every mineral. The paper is strongest for solution chemistry/environmental transport, not engineering capacity comparisons.

Adsorbent / material: Illitic, kaolinitic and lateritic soil clays
Continuum stage: Natural minerals / clay interaction; data-quality caveat
Experimental design / conditions: The abstract and Fig. 2(c) are the relevant source locations; supplementary Table S1 was not included in the uploaded PDF set.
Reported result: The abstract states the OTC sorption-capacity order as illitic soil clay > kaolinitic soil clay > lateritic soil clay. Visual inspection of Fig. 2(c) appears to show kaolinitic > illitic > lateritic in both the deionized-water and seawater groups.
Value / units: Do not use an exact numerical rank pending verification
Model / metric: Text-versus-figure discrepancy; figure values are not extracted numerically
Caveat / follow-up: Preserve this discrepancy explicitly. Avoid repeating the abstract's ranking as established until checked against supplementary material or author clarification.

Adsorbent / material: Fe3O4 magnetic core coated with siliceous shells enriched in alginic-acid-, ι-carrageenan- or κ-carrageenan-derived groups
Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Magnetite cores synthesized by hydrolytic oxidation of Fe(II) in alkaline medium. Alginic acid was modified with tributylamine (TBA); alginic acid and carrageenans were derivatized with ICPTES; a shell was formed using TEOS and polysaccharide-derived silane reagents; particles were washed with ethanol.
Reported result: The products are engineered magnetic nanosorbents, not unmodified alginate/carrageenan and not pristine biochar. Their design combines magnetite-assisted separation with silica and biopolymer functional groups.
Model / metric: Preparation-route characterization, not an adsorption performance metric
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–3 (printed pp. 828–829), Methods; PDF pp. 4–5 (printed pp. 830–831), characterization
Caveat / follow-up: Processing involves several chemical reagents and solvent washing. The supplied main text provides no harmonized preparation cost or LCA; do not imply that high capacity necessarily means low overall cost.

Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Table 1 reports TEM particle/core-shell dimensions and BET surface area.
Reported result: Magnetite core diameter was 50 ± 8 nm. Shell thicknesses were 15 ± 2 nm (alginate-derived), 7 ± 1 nm (ι-carrageenan-derived) and 23 ± 3 nm (κ-carrageenan-derived). BET areas were 34.4 m²/g for Fe3O4, 16.1 m²/g for alginate-derived particles, 24.7 m²/g for ι-carrageenan-derived particles and 26.3 m²/g for κ-carrageenan-derived particles.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 5 (printed p. 831), Table 1; PDF pp. 4–5, Fig. 1
Caveat / follow-up: Coating lowers BET surface area relative to bare Fe3O4, so capacity differences should not be attributed to surface area alone. Supporting Table S1 contains additional detail not supplied here.

Adsorbent / material: Magnetic alginate- and carrageenan-based siliceous nanosorbents
Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Initial CIP concentration 50 mg/L; contact time 24 h; pH varied from 2 to 9. Figure 3 reports removal versus pH.
Reported result: ι-carrageenan-derived particles reached approximately 95% removal at pH 3; κ-carrageenan-derived particles were around 20% at pH 3. Alginate-derived particles showed about 75–85% removal between pH 3 and 6, with a maximum near 85% at pH 5. Removal fell above pH 6 for the ι-carrageenan and alginate materials; κ-carrageenan removal remained comparatively low in this pH profile.
Value / units: Approximate removal percentages from the source plot and narrative; not qmax
Model / metric: Removal (%) at one initial concentration and contact time
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 7 (printed p. 833), Fig. 3 and Section 3.2.1
Evidence status: Extracted from main text and figure
Caveat / follow-up: Use only with the stated 50 mg/L and 24 h context. These pH-profile values are not comparable to isotherm-derived capacities.

Adsorbent / material: Fe3O4@SiO2/SiTBA-ALG; Fe3O4@SiO2/SiιCRG; Fe3O4@SiO2/SiκCRG; bare Fe3O4 comparator
Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic tests used 5 mg sorbent in 10 mL CIP solution at initial concentrations of 50, 100 and 200 mg/L, pH 5, 25 ± 2 °C and 30 rpm; monitored up to 24 h.
Reported result: Carrageenan-derived particles reached their plateau after about 30 min. Alginate-derived particles plateaued after about 5 h at the lowest concentration and required up to 24 h at higher concentrations. The paper reports maximum removal of about 88% (alginate) and 90% (ι-carrageenan) at 50 mg/L; κ-carrageenan removal was about 30% at 200 mg/L. Bare Fe3O4 gave about 6% removal and a reported qmax of 5.4 mg/g.
Value / units: Removal (%) and reported bare-Fe3O4 qmax = 5.4 mg/g
Model / metric: Time-profile and removal data; different initial feeds retained separately
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3 and 8 (printed pp. 829 and 834), Methods and Fig. 4 / Section 3.2.2
Evidence status: Extracted from main text and figure
Caveat / follow-up: The qmax comparator for bare Fe3O4 is not accompanied in the paragraph with its full condition set; do not use as a same-condition benchmark without checking Fig. S10/SI. Concentration and material-specific results remain separate.

Adsorbent / material: Alginate-, ι-carrageenan- and κ-carrageenan-derived magnetic nanosorbents
Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, Elovich and Boyd models were fitted; detailed parameter tables are in supplementary Tables S3–S5 and Fig. S11, not supplied.
Reported result: The authors report pseudo-second-order fits with R² between 0.95 and 0.99 and low chi-square values. Boyd plots did not pass through the origin, which the authors interpret as evidence against intraparticle diffusion being the sole rate-limiting step; they propose film diffusion and/or surface reaction contributes.
Model / metric: Model fit and Boyd plot interpretation
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 8–9 (printed pp. 834–835), Section 3.2.3; supporting Tables S3–S5 and Fig. S11 referenced
Evidence status: Extracted from main text; SI not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: Pseudo-second-order fit quality alone does not establish a unique chemical mechanism. Do not state chemisorption as proven solely from the model fit.

Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm tests: 1.5 mg sorbent in 3 mL CIP solutions with initial concentrations 50–1200 mg/L, pH 5, 25 °C and 24 h. Equilibrium capacity calculated by solution mass balance.
Reported result: Table 2 reports qmax = 463.7 mg/g for alginate-derived particles and 426.6 mg/g for ι-carrageenan-derived particles, both marked as maximum Langmuir capacities. For κ-carrageenan-derived particles Table 2 reports 1350.1 mg/g; the body states the Dubinin–Radushkevich model fit these data best (R² = 0.9694), while Langmuir and Freundlich fits were poor (R² < 0.9).
Value / units: qmax: 463.7 mg/g (Langmuir, alginate); 426.6 mg/g (Langmuir, ι-carrageenan); 1350.1 mg/g (D–R-based value for κ-carrageenan)
Model / metric: Fitted model capacities; first two Langmuir; κ-carrageenan best described by D–R
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3 and 9–10 (printed pp. 829 and 835–836), isotherm methods/results; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 838), Table 2
Caveat / follow-up: The abstract gives 423 mg/g for ι-carrageenan, the results prose says 427 mg/g, and Table 2 reports 426.6 mg/g. Preserve this discrepancy; Table 2 value is transcribed as reported but not silently reconciled. Initial concentrations are high (50–1200 mg/L); do not compare directly with low-environmental-concentration removal.

Adsorbent / material: Alginate-, ι-carrageenan- and κ-carrageenan-derived magnetic nanosorbents
Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Four consecutive adsorption/desorption cycles; CIP desorption induced using 1 M KCl. For loading, 5 mg particles in 10 mL feed; initial CIP 50 mg/L for alginate/ι-carrageenan materials and 200 mg/L for κ-carrageenan particles.
Reported result: The paper reports alginate- and ι-carrageenan-derived sorbents at about 99–96 mg/g in cycle 1 and 97–90 mg/g after cycle 4 (<5% decrease). For κ-carrageenan, capacity decreases from 133 to 106 mg/g after the first regeneration step and is 101 mg/g after four cycles.
Value / units: Cycle capacities (mg/g), not maximum isotherm capacities
Model / metric: Four adsorption/desorption cycles using KCl regeneration
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 12 (printed p. 838), Section 3.2.5 and Fig. 6; SI Figs. S13–S14 referenced
Evidence status: Extracted; cycle values and differing loading conditions kept separate
Caveat / follow-up: Do not equate cycle capacities with fitted qmax values in EV-012. Initial loading concentration differs for κ-carrageenan. No regenerant pollutant mass balance or regeneration-waste cost is reported in the supplied main text.

Adsorbent / material: Anionic carboxylate groups of alginate and ester-sulfate groups of carrageenan on silica-coated magnetite
Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: pH-dependent removal, surface characterization/FTIR shifts, isotherm fitting and D–R energy analysis.
Reported result: The authors attribute uptake mainly to electrostatic interactions between protonated CIP and anionic polysaccharide groups; hydrogen bonding is also proposed. For κ-carrageenan, D–R E = 10.83 kJ/mol is interpreted as consistent with ion exchange. For alginate and ι-carrageenan, reported D–R E values are 101 and 110 kJ/mol respectively and are interpreted by the authors as chemisorption/electrostatic interaction.
Value / units: Reported D–R E: 10.83, 101 and 110 kJ/mol for κ-carrageenan, alginate and ι-carrageenan respectively
Model / metric: Model-based energy interpretation plus FTIR shifts; not unique mechanistic proof
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 9–11 (printed pp. 835–837), Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4; PDF pp. 11–12, FTIR discussion
Caveat / follow-up: Model-derived energy estimates should be reported as the authors' interpretation, not direct observation. Supporting Table S8 and spectral figures are referenced but SI was not supplied.

Continuum stage: Chemically modified biopolymer / magnetic silica nanocomposite
Experimental design / conditions: Adsorption experiments use prepared aqueous CIP solutions; no real wastewater test or cost/LCA study is presented in the supplied main paper.
Reported result: Magnetic core supports separation with an external magnet; reuse was examined for four adsorption/desorption cycles. The study does not establish performance in real wastewater, low ng/L–µg/L matrices, or a harmonized process cost or life-cycle benefit.
Value / units: Not reported: real-water performance, preparation cost, LCA, complete spent-regenerant balance
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1–3 (study aim and methods); PDF pp. 12–13 (reuse/conclusion)
Caveat / follow-up: Absence is limited to the supplied main paper; supplementary materials were not reviewed. Do not infer real-wastewater performance or lower total cost from the projected application.
